Appendix C • Approximate Velocity Units in Single-Snapshot Calculations [3.2.3]

C.3 Relation to the implementation used in fake_spectra

The practical implementation used in fake_spectra adopts directly the velocity-space point of view. The spectrum is discretized on a uniform velocity grid, \begin{align} u_n=n\,\Delta u, \qquad \Delta u=\frac{u_{\max}}{N_{\mathrm{bins}}}, \tag{C.18} \end{align} with total span \begin{align} u_{\max}=L_{\mathrm{box}}\,v_{\mathrm{fac}}, \tag{C.19} \end{align} where \(L_{\mathrm{box}}\) is the box size along the line of sight and \(v_{\mathrm{fac}}\) is the conversion factor from comoving box units to physical \(\mathrm{km}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}\). In continuum notation, this corresponds to the approximation \begin{align} u_H^{\mathrm{FS}}(x) \approx \frac{H(z_{\mathrm{box}})}{1+z_{\mathrm{box}}}\,x, \tag{C.20} \end{align} where the choice of origin is fixed implicitly by the box coordinate convention.

Each gas element is then moved to redshift space by adding its line-of-sight peculiar velocity: \begin{align} u_{\mathrm{abs}}^{\mathrm{FS}}(x) = u_H^{\mathrm{FS}}(x) + v_{i\,\parallel}^{\mathrm{FS}}(x). \tag{C.21} \end{align} This is the specific sign convention adopted by the code. If one uses the opposite sign convention for \(v_{i\,\parallel}\), the same physical construction would instead be written with a minus sign. Thus, the apparent sign difference should be interpreted only as a matter of convention, not as a difference in the underlying physics.

In this implementation, the line profile is not evaluated by first constructing an explicit frequency offset. Instead, one works directly with the velocity-space detuning \begin{align} \Delta u^{\mathrm{FS}}(x;u) = u-u_{\mathrm{abs}}^{\mathrm{FS}}(x), \tag{C.22} \end{align} and with the corresponding dimensionless quantity \begin{align} y_{ij}(x;u) = \frac{\Delta u^{\mathrm{FS}}(x;u)}{b_i(x)}, \tag{C.23} \end{align} where \(b_i(x)\) is the local Doppler width parameter. The Voigt/Faddeeva kernel may then be written schematically as \begin{align} \phi_{ij}(x,u) \propto \Re\!\left[ \mathcal W\!\left( y_{ij}(x;u)+i\,a_{ij}(x) \right) \right], \tag{C.24} \end{align} where \(a_{ij}(x)\) is the corresponding dimensionless damping parameter.

Thus, the practical optical-depth calculation may be viewed schematically as \begin{align} \tau_{ij}(u) \propto \int dx\; n_i(x)\, \phi_{ij}(x,u) = \int dx\; n_i(x)\, \phi_{ij}\!\left( u-u_{\mathrm{abs}}^{\mathrm{FS}}(x) \right), \tag{C.25} \end{align} up to the appropriate normalization factors and kernel-weighting details. This makes explicit the central idea of the implementation: the spectrum is sampled on a universal velocity grid, each absorber is assigned a redshift-space position on that grid, and the line profile depends only on the difference between the pixel coordinate and the absorber-centered coordinate.

Finally, note that this practical velocity grid is universal: it is not redefined separately for each transition. The dependence on the specific line \(j\) enters through the rest-frame wavelength, the oscillator strength, the damping coefficient, and the thermal/microturbulent broadening parameters, but the spectral axis itself is common to all transitions.
